This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
summary: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

title: Planet formation on solar system scales
summary: Giant planets are often regarded as primordial protoplanetary "architects". Their formation and interactions with planetesimals and other planets during and after the protoplanetary disc phase are key to setting the blueprint of the planetary systems we observe today. Catching nascent gas giants is our best opportunity to uncover these crucial steps in the planet formation process and shed light on the origins of our own solar system. Over the last decade, ALMA has revolutionised our understanding of planet formation; still, detecting signatures of Jupiter-like planets has remained out of reach. We argue that ALMA2040, a next-generation sub(mm) interferometer with improved sensitivity ($\times25$ in the continuum and $\times10$ for line emission) and a $\times3$ higher angular resolution compared to ALMA, will be sensitive to (sub)mm emission around a forming Jupiter-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star within $150\,{\rm pc}$ and allow kinematically characterising interactions of Jovian and sub-Jovian planets with their natal disc. ALMA2040 will provide unique and unprecedented insights into how gas giants carve gaps, accrete material, form satellites, and affect the architectures of their co-evolving planetary systems.

title: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
summary: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.

title: In-Context Learning Before Specialisation: Theory of Learning in a Solvable Topic Model
summary: Sequence models can generalise in fundamentally distinct ways: extrapolating structures seen in training, or using their prompt to adapt to novel tasks. The prevailing strategy determines how the model behaves beyond its training distribution, controlling potential capabilities and risks. Recent work has characterised many different strategies theoretically, and empirically described the transition between them as the quality and quantity of pretraining data vary. However, there is no learning theory for this competition, hence no fundamental understanding of \textit{why} one solution might be favoured over another. Here we provide such a theory in a solvable topic model---documents drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data. The dataset comes with two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor, that stores the finite topic mixture, and an in-context one, optimal for topics never seen during training. Our theory predicts their emergence at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor is available early, while the specialised one emerges only after the training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the separating crossover in remarkable agreement with the theory, with no fitted parameters.

title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
summary: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.

title: Cutoff Phenomenon for the Glauber-Misanthrope process in a perturbative regime
summary:
We investigate the Glauber--Misanthrope process, obtained by superposing a Misanthrope dynamics with finite site capacity and a Glauber dynamics which creates or annihilates particles one at a time at each site. In a perturbative regime around the diffusively scaled partial exclusion process, we prove the cutoff phenomenon and identify the limiting mixing time.
  Our approach relies on the information percolation framework developed by Lubetzky and Sly and extended by Tran, which we adapt to accommodate multiple occupancy per site and account for the two distinct correlation mechanisms generated by the Misanthrope and Glauber dynamics. Our lower bound on the mixing time holds under assumptions more general than those required for the matching upper bound.

title: Lossy Lorentz boosts at ultra-relativistic energies: Numerical study and source survey of high-energy physics software
summary:
Most high-energy-physics software packages implement Lorentz boosts for themselves. At sufficiently large boosts, these routines can return finite, plausible-looking four-vectors whose invariant masses and rest-frame properties are no longer accurate. We survey implementations in widely used collider and air-shower software and compare representative algorithms in three numerical tests.
  We find that the main problem is usually information discarded by the representation, rather than the arithmetic of the boost formula. Information can be lost when a boost is specified only by its velocity, and again when the result is stored only through Cartesian components. Richer boost input prevents the first loss, while retaining light-cone coordinates prevents the second. Ordinary hard processes at present colliders are safe in double precision; the relevant regimes are low-mass systems, highly boosted auxiliary frames, single-precision particle records and air-shower simulations. Extreme scale hierarchies in parton-shower accuracy tests and ultra-heavy particle decays provide still more demanding cases.

title: Rank Measures of Fine-Tuning Updates Need a Noise Baseline
summary: Studies of what fine-tuning does to a language model often summarise the weight update $ΔW$ by its rank. We compare the rank measures used for this against the same measures on a random matrix of the same shape, and against two harder references: the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content. Measures that count directions put our fine-tuning updates only a little below noise; stable rank, computed from the same singular values, puts them far below. Both are right: an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds for thirteen released pairs up to 8B parameters, and it is not a mark of alignment: with training held fixed, instruction data does not stand out from Wikipedia or code, DPO gives the same update whether its preference labels are real or half swapped at random (one model, modest preference strength), and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update of all. Applied to a recent claim that post-training is superficial because the effective rank of the weights barely changes, the baselines show that a random update of the same size leaves that rank almost unchanged while wrecking the model, and that an edit built on the effective rank of the update has no measurable effect in our tests. Rank measures of weight updates need a noise baseline, and claims about alignment need a control without alignment content.

title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
summary: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.

title: From Scaling Relations to Physical Laws: Constraining the Physics of Star Formation Across Local Galaxies
summary: The conversion of cold dense gas, traced by molecular line emission, into stars remains one of the fundamental unsolved problems in galaxy evolution. Observations over the past decades have established empirical relations between gas and star formation, yet their physical origin remains uncertain. Gravity, turbulence, and stellar feedback as main drivers provide fundamentally different pictures of how star formation is regulated, while reproducing remarkably similar galaxy-scale scaling relations. To disentangle the individual importance of each process, not only its mass and distribution, but also its temperature, density, excitation, and chemistry must be probed. However, current or planned (sub)millimetre facilities cannot combine statistical breadth, cloud-scale resolution, and multi-line diagnostics across large galaxy samples. A new, flagship interferometer with increased line sensitivity and bandwidth enables obtaining multi-transition, multi-isotopologue observations of molecular gas at GMC-resolved scales across nearby galaxies, enabling millions of independent measurements of its physical state across a wide range of extragalactic environments. This will transform molecular gas from an empirical tracer into a quantitative probe of the physical processes governing the relation between the dense gas and star formation. With the 2040s landscape of optical and radio facilities, ALMA2040 will facilitate a predictive theory of the conversion of gas into stars.

title: Low-Scale See-Saw Mechanism and the Majorana Nature of Heavy Neutrinos
summary: We investigate the possibility to determine the Majorana nature of the heavy Majorana neutrinos present in the low-scale type I seesaw mechanism of neutrino mass generation in experiments at $e^+ \text{-} e^-$ and $μ^+ \text{-} μ^-$ colliders. This is done on the examples of two specific symmetry-protected seesaw scenarios with two right-handed (RH) singlet neutrinos and one seesaw realization with three RH neutrinos. We use the forward-backward symmetry in the angular distribution of the heavy neutral leptons produced in the $e^+ \text{-} e^-$ and $μ^+ \text{-} μ^-$ collisions as an indicator of their Majorana nature. Our results indicate that the experiments at FCCee during its first phase of operation have a remarkable potential not only to discover the heavy neutral leptons associated with the type I seesaw mechanism if they have masses smaller than the $Z^0$-boson mass, but also to probe and provide evidence for their Majorana nature.

title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.

title: Aligning LLMs with Sparse Retrieval via Adaptive Sparse Supervision
summary: While large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic representations, their application to first-stage retrieval incurs substantial latency and storage costs. Neural sparse retrievers such as SPLADE provide efficient retrieval but rely on relatively compact encoders with limited representational capacity. To bridge this gap, we propose an LLM-based sparse retrieval framework with input-adaptive sparse alignment. Specifically, we introduce a dynamic $α$-truncation strategy that selects input-specific supervision supports based on the cumulative activation mass of SPLADE representations. This strategy guides the LLM to preserve salient lexical signals while suppressing less informative activations, without relying on a fixed support budget. Subsequent retrieval fine-tuning combines contrastive learning, knowledge distillation, and sparsity regularization to improve retrieval effectiveness. Experiments on MS MARCO and six selected BEIR datasets demonstrate improvements over SPLADE++ while maintaining competitive effectiveness against LLM-based sparse retrievers. Compared with Lion-sp, our method reduces index storage by 6.4-fold and end-to-end query latency by over 11-fold, achieving a favorable effectiveness-efficiency trade-off.

title: Provably Efficient Risk-Sensitive Offline Reinforcement Learning via Optimized Certainty Equivalents
summary: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

title: Convective Oscillations of Cosmic Rays
summary: Turbulent motion of the background plasma can introduce fluctuations in the spatial distribution of cosmic rays (CRs). For an ensemble-averaged Gaussian CR distribution with a width $ Λ\left( t,p \right) $ at time $ t $ and momentum $ p $, it is found that $ P_\text{s}\left( t,k,p \right) $ and $ P_\text{d}\left( t,k,p \right) $, the fluctuation power spectra induced by incompressible and acoustic turbulent convection, respectively, have power-law asymptotics in wavenumber $ k $: $ P_\text{s}\left( t,k,p \right) \propto k^4 $ and $ P_\text{d}\left( t,k,p \right) \propto k^2 $ for $ k\ll 1/Λ\left( t,p \right) $; $ P_\text{s}\left( t,k,p \right) \propto k^{γ_\text{s}-4} $ for $ k\gg 1/L_\text{s} $, and $ P_\text{d}\left( t,k,p \right) \propto k^{γ_\text{d}-2} $ for $ k\gg 1/L_\text{d} $, where $ γ_\text{s} $ and $ γ_\text{d} $ are the spectral indices of the velocity power spectra of the incompressible and acoustic turbulence below their outer scales $ L_\text{s} $ and $ L_\text{d} $, respectively. These results have implications for probing interstellar turbulence via future high-resolution images of pulsar gamma-ray halos.

title: From Accelerating Rotating Black Holes to a Swirling Universe
summary: We demonstrate that the swirling universe can be recovered through a coordinated horizon-degeneration and scaling procedure applied to the Kerr C-metric. The construction exploits the horizon structure of accelerating, rotating black holes, which allows their inner and outer horizons to coalesce while simultaneously approaching the acceleration horizon. By magnifying the near-acceleration-horizon region faster than the black hole horizons approach it, the pair of accelerating, rotating black holes is pushed to an infinite proper distance, while a finite gravitomagnetic twist survives. The resulting geometry reproduces precisely the swirling universe, providing a physical interpretation of its intrinsic rotation as the gravitational remnant of rotating black holes sent to infinity.

title: Evolved stars: dust formation and mass loss
summary: Evolved stars drive the chemical enrichment of the Universe, acting as primary producers of elemental products of nucleosynthesis and cosmic dust. Unraveling the exact role played by these objects requires empirical constraints on the interplay between pulsation, convection, magnetic fields, mass loss, and dust formation at small (milliarcsecond) scales, currently limited to only a handful of sources. Next-generation facilities, particularly the new ALMA2040, will enable systematic, spatially resolved studies of mass loss and dust formation across large samples of evolved stars, expanding from a few tens to hundreds of objects and providing the empirical constraints needed to understand the recycling and chemical enrichment of baryonic matter throughout the Universe.

title: Seeing Both the Forest and the Trees: Reusing Holistic 3D Priors for Part-Decomposed Generation
summary: Generating 3D assets with explicit parts requires two properties at once: geometric detail inside each part and structural coherence across the whole object. Recent image-conditioned 3D generation models adopt a structured 3D representation that anchors tokens to explicit spatial positions, capturing both properties, but their output remains a single fused mesh. We ask how a part-decomposed generation model can inherit both properties of these holistic priors, and answer with STRUCTPARTS, a framework whose core technical contribution is a dual-frame coordinate interleaving mechanism: each shape latent is interpreted under both a part-local and an object-global reference frame, and processed through a global-local inter-leaved transformer that simultaneously reuses the prior's geometric detail at the part scale and its structural coherence at the whole-object scale. As its structural input, STRUCTPARTS uses a segmented mesh scaffold, a coarse mesh paired with a face-level segmentation mask kept entirely within the prior's native 3D representation. With only lightweight finetuning, both intra-part detail and inter-part coherence emerge from the same pretrained weights. On PartObjaverse-Tiny, STRUCTPARTS matches or surpasses prior part-decomposed models at a fraction of their training cost, while naturally supporting part-mesh refinement and part-level editing.

title: Frontiers of chemical complexity in the interstellar medium: unveiling the cosmic origins of life
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) contains a rich molecular inventory that provides a unique window into the chemistry operating during star and planet formation and its connection to prebiotic chemistry. More than 350 interstellar molecules are currently known, including increasingly complex organic molecules and species containing elements beyond the second row of the periodic table. Yet the limits that interstellar chemical complexity can reach, its evolution from molecular clouds to planetary systems, and its contribution to the molecular feedstock of life remain poorly constrained. Addressing these questions requires sensitive, broadband observations capable of detecting multiple weak rotational transitions of molecular species, such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars and lipids, towards star- and planet-forming environments. Current facilities, including ALMA, are limited by instantaneous spectral coverage, sensitivity (especially on extended spatial scales), and the trade-off between total bandwidth and integration time. The proposed ALMA2040 facility would overcome these limitations through at least a tenfold improvement in spectral-line sensitivity, high-fidelity imaging from sub-arcsecond to tens-of-arcsecond scales, and ultra-broad instantaneous frequency coverage from 35 to 950 GHz at high spectral resolution. These capabilities would allow systematic detections of species with molecular abundances with respect to H$_2$ below 10$^{-11}$, facilitating the identification of new complex and heavy-element-bearing species through multiple transitions, and providing complete molecular inventories across evolutionary stages. ALMA2040 would thus make it possible to comprehensively investigate the emergence and evolution of chemical complexity, and to determine whether molecular precursors of prebiotic chemistry are widespread throughout the Galaxy.

title: Photon-Return and Polar-Focusing Crossovers near Extremal Kerr
summary: How precisely must a photon's impact parameter be tuned for it to complete $n$ windings around a nearly extremal Kerr black hole before escaping, and how does the same near extremal scaling control the focusing of neighboring rays? For equatorial prograde returns we find, with $κ=\sqrt{1-a^2/M^2}$ and $X=nκ$, $ε_n=\sqrt{3}\,κ/(e^{2πX}-1) +O(κ^2|\lnκ|)$. This single law connects the extremal inverse-winding hierarchy to subextremal exponential accumulation. Perturbing the return family quasi-equatorially, we derive a second scaling law for the polar Jacobi phase, $Ψ_θ=2\ln[\sinh(πX)/κ]+C_s+o(1)$, and show that its focusing points cross from geometric spacing in winding number to asymptotically uniform spacing $Δ\mathcal N\simeq(2κ)^{-1}$. Numerical integrations of the exact Kerr radial dynamics and linear polar equation verify both scaling collapses. Thus near extremal Kerr exhibits parametrically distinct winding and polar-focusing scales, rather than a discontinuous jump between extremal and subextremal lensing hierarchies.

title: A general feedback mechanism unifying stochasticity, long transients, and resilience
summary: Stochasticity in complex systems is commonly treated either as external noise added to deterministic dynamics or as an effective stochastic description of deterministic chaos. A framework in which stochastic dynamics arise endogenously from deterministic chaos and subsequently feed back on the deterministic dynamics, thereby fundamentally reshaping system dynamics, remains rare. Here, we develop such a framework. Through the interaction between deterministic and stochastic dynamics, alternative stable states, critical transitions, adaptive capacity, stochasticity, and resilience become dynamically interconnected within a single model. Furthermore, the framework establishes a new mechanism of long transients, driven by two key factors: (i) time-scale separation and (ii) time-delay-induced cancellation. Stochasticity plays a dual stabilizing-destabilizing role in long transients: it promotes their persistence while also facilitating their eventual escape and collapse. This dual role allows resilience to be quantified dynamically through escape and stochastic recapture dynamics. Finally, we establish the generality of the mechanism mathematically and numerically across a broad class of one-dimensional nonlinear systems, suggesting that it reflects a general dynamical principle.

title: Physics-Aware Distillation of a Grid Foundation Model for Real-Time Edge Inference
summary: Grid foundation models (GridFMs) are graph transformers pretrained on a masked power-flow objective, and evaluate power flow orders of magnitude faster than an iterative solver. Their size, however, targets data-centre inference, whereas low-inertia operation increasingly asks for inference at the edge, next to the measurement, at batch size one and within a single synchrophasor (PMU) reporting frame. We distil a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer GridFM teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student, a $32.5\times$ parameter reduction at half the message-passing depth, using an objective that combines the masked power-flow loss with output, physics-residual, latent-state and attention transfer. The physics-residual term, which matches the teacher's power-residual profile, has not previously been applied to typed power-grid graphs. We evaluate on a renewable variant of the IEEE 118-bus benchmark grid in which 26 of the conventional (synchronous) generators are replaced by inverter-based renewables with battery flexibility and standardised reactive-power limits (IEEE 1547), giving $97\,529$ physically valid (AC-OPF-feasible) operating scenarios, and we ablate all eight combinations of the transfer terms, reporting accuracy against ground truth and fidelity to the teacher separately. Distillation lowers student error on all four predicted quantities, by up to $48\%$ on active-power dispatch, and every distilled student is more accurate than its teacher on reactive-power dispatch. The gain is largely carried by the output matching term. The physics-residual term, in the layer-aggregated form used here, is consistently harmful, which we attribute to the spatial averaging it applies to a bus-level residual field. The resulting student is $32.5\times$ smaller in parameter count and has half the message-passing depth, making it a candidate for subsequent edge-device benchmarking.

title: Thermodynamics of rotating black holes with constrained primary hair
summary: An exact rotating geometry need not define a black hole in equilibrium when its surface gravity varies across the horizon. We construct an asymptotically flat, non-Kerr subfamily of the aligned null solutions of generalized Proca theory whose outer horizon is exactly Killing and isothermal to second order in rotation. The horizon conditions constrain the vector hair, and integrability of the normalized horizon charge fixes the remaining second-order amplitude. Computing the complete gravitational and nonminimal vector surface charges, we obtain the asymptotically normalized mass and total angular momentum, and derive a logarithmic Hamiltonian entropy. The first law holds in both independent directions of the resulting two-parameter solution space. We express the mass as a function of entropy and angular momentum, recover the geometric thermodynamic potentials, and establish a scale-corrected Smarr relation that retains the dimensionful coupling. The exact metric defines the geometry, while equilibrium thermodynamics is consistently restricted to second order in spin.

title: Finite Time Noncollapsing Kähler-Ricci Flow: Gaussian Type Heat Kernel, Gromov-Hausdorff Limits
summary:
In this paper, we study heat kernel estimates along the Kähler-Ricci flow with finite time noncollapsing singularities over a compact Kähler manifold. The starting point is the type-II scalar-curvature estimate, which gives the natural parabolic scale $r\lesssim T-t$ near the singular time. By combining the distance distortion and space-time cut-off estimates of Bamler--Zhang with entropy, mean-value inequality, and conjugate heat-kernel estimates, we obtain two-sided Gaussian bounds and gradient bounds that are uniform on this scale. Under the global type-I scalar-curvature estimate, the same estimates hold on every scale.
  We then use these estimates and the monotonicity of the $W_1$-distance between conjugate heat flows to construct a canonical singular-time pseudo-distance. The distances $d_t$ (induced by $ω(t)$) converge uniformly to this pseudo-distance. Its metric quotient is the unique Gromov--Hausdorff limit.
  Finally, we apply Bamler's theory and the recent work of Hallgren--Zhang to obtain the following. Every fixed-base-point type-I blow-up admits a subsequential metric-flow limit whose time slices are singular shrinking Kähler--Ricci soliton spaces with normal complex-analytic and log-terminal structure, unique tangent cones, and a polarized Fano fibration. For moving base points, the limiting metric flow, equipped with its limiting conjugate heat flow, is a metric soliton precisely under an entropy-pinching condition.

title: A Closed Form Depth-Width Law for Neural Collapse in Deep Linear Networks
summary: How depth and width of neural networks shape learned representations is usually studied only after training. We show that, in a tractable feature-learning setting, this dependence can instead be obtained in closed form. Using neural collapse as a probe of representation geometry, we express NC1--NC3 directly in terms of the learned feature kernel, extending an identity known for NC1 to the angular part of NC2 and to NC3 under a ridge readout. For deep linear networks with exchangeable class structure, the resulting kernel equations yield a geometric law, exact within the theory, for the layerwise evolution of within-class variability. At large width, the accumulated compression becomes a function of the depth-to-width ratio $L/N$, with its rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior and architecture. Numerical experiments support the derived dependence on depth, width and signal-to-noise ratio. The result is a representation-level scaling law derived from feature-learning theory rather than fitted after training.

title: Exact Makespan Bounds and the GPipe Homogeneity Bias for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Pipelines
summary: We give an exact critical-path characterization of the makespan of micro-batch pipelines serving LLMs on heterogeneous GPU clusters, quantifying how the classic homogeneous GPipe formula errs. In the pure-forward, communication-free, infinite-buffer setting, T(M) = (M-1)tau_max + Sum_j tau_j, where tau_j is stage j's per-micro-batch service time and M the micro-batch count (Theorem 1). Under asynchronous communication -- modern NCCL-based serving -- it extends to T(M) = Sum_j tau_j + Sum_j d_j + (M-1)tau_max, with Sum_j d_j a purely additive constant (Theorem 2); under blocking communication, T(M) = (M-1)sigma_max + Sum_s sigma_s with sigma_s = tau_s + d_s, so communication enters the steady-state slope iff some d_s > tau_max - tau_s (Theorem 3). These results quantify the GPipe overestimate, decompose the bias into a homogeneity term Sum_j (tau_max - tau_j) and a communication-ignoring term Sum_j d_j, and imply that balancing per-stage compute dominates communication reduction for steady-state throughput. A real system with partial overlap is sandwiched between Theorems 2 and 3, with a closed-form bound on the overlap throughput gain. All claims are validated pointwise (error < 10^-9) on eleven configurations and a 1.6x10^5-point fuzz, including a mixed RTX 5090/3090/GTX 1070 partition. We situate the results in flow-shop scheduling and list open extensions: bandwidth-limited communication, bounded buffers, prefill-decode interleaving.

title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.

title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
summary: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.

title: Extracting the Central Sound Speed of Neutron Stars through Intrinsic Stellar Structure Scaling with Reduced Equation-of-State Model Dependence
summary: Inferring neutron star (NS) core properties remains sensitive to the assumed equation of state (EOS). Using a nonlinear Walecka model with generalized $ω$-meson self-interactions, we construct six EOS families, each containing $10^3$ samples subject to identical nuclear and astrophysical constraints. Despite satisfying these constraints, the families predict markedly different high-density behavior and core properties; higher-order $ω$ interactions can also generate interior sound-speed peaks within purely nucleonic matter. To reduce this model dependence, we use the intrinsic and perturbative analysis of the dimensionless Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff equations (IPAD-TOV) to derive an EOS-independent estimator $Θ(\rm{X},Ψ)$ of the central squared sound speed $s_{\rm c}^2$, where $\rm{X}=P_{\rm c}/\varepsilon_{\rm c}$ is the central EOS-parameter and $Ψ$ characterizes the stellar-mass response to central energy density. For canonical $1.4\,M_\odot$ NSs, $Θ$ correlates linearly with $s_{\rm c}^2$ across the families ($R^2\approx0.94$-$0.99$). The family-dependent relations converge toward a common optimum: minimizing their dispersion yields $s_{\rm c}^2\approx 0.523\pm0.044$ and $\rm{X}\approx 0.173^{+0.020}_{-0.018}$ for all six families, or $s_{\rm c}^2\approx 0.496\pm0.092$ and $\rm{X}\approx 0.167^{+0.030}_{-0.029}$ when the family without $ω$ self-interaction is excluded. The corresponding radii are $11.73^{+1.08}_{-0.92}$ and $11.92^{+1.76}_{-1.28}\,\rm km$, respectively, with $95\%$ confidence intervals. A unified scaling fitted to all EOS samples supports both extractions. These results show how common stellar-structure relations can constrain NS core properties with reduced EOS-model dependence, even when existing observations cannot distinguish among the underlying EOS descriptions.

title: Rethinking Batch Composition: Promoting Feature Diversity for Speech Enhancement
summary: Speech enhancement systems are commonly trained using randomly sampled mini-batches, which may contain limited diversity in intrinsic acoustic characteristics of the clean speech signals. Motivated by previous findings linking clean speech characteristics to enhancement performance, we propose a feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that divides training examples into quantiles according to a clean-speech characteristic and enforces equal representation within each mini-batch. Experiments across two large-scale English and Spanish speech datasets and a smaller dataset containing neurotypical and pathological speech demonstrate improvements over standard random mini-batch sampling across multiple objective enhancement metrics. Ablation studies demonstrate that the gains are robust across training runs, while their magnitude depends on the acoustic characteristic used for stratification. The proposed strategy requires no modification to the enhancement model or training objective, providing a simple and complementary approach to speech enhancement training.

title: Behavioral Forgetting Is Not Privacy in Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information from large language models, but existing evaluations often measure forgetting only on a designated benchmark distribution. We argue that such behavioral forgetting is an insufficient standard for privacy-oriented unlearning, and that evaluation should instead test whether forgetting persists across the access paths through which the same information may be recovered. We demonstrate this with a controlled case study of cross-lingual querying: across multiple multilingual model families, forgetting varies substantially when semantically equivalent information is queried in different languages and scripts. A single access path is therefore enough to expose a real gap between behavioral forgetting and information inaccessibility, motivating broader evaluation of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability alongside in-distribution forgetting.

title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation
summary: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.

title: MedPAO-VL: Interpretable and Protocol-Compliant Agent for Structured Radiology Report Generation
summary: Despite the remarkable generalization capabilities of Large Language Models, generating clinically accurate and structured radiology reports from medical images remains a significant challenge. Current end-to-end approaches function as black boxes, prone to factual hallucinations and generating ungrounded findings. This lack of reliability and failure to adhere to domain-specific structuring protocols, fundamentally limits their clinical utility. We present MedPAO-VL, a multimodal agent that shifts the paradigm from monolithic generation to explainable, iterative, protocol-compliant structured report generation. Unlike deterministic models, our plan-act-observe loop functions as a goal-oriented agent: it first perceives the Chest X-Ray through an explainable vision module designed to capture inherent diagnostic uncertainty, then iteratively refines the generated report by observing semantic discrepancies and self-correcting its generation for better alignment with visually detected clinical findings. Evaluation of our framework demonstrates that this agentic reasoning improves clinical correctness and completeness, achieving an expert-rated accuracy score of 3.5/5 and a structural score of 4.3/5. By prioritizing pathology specific explainability and iterative refinement over opaque end-to-end mapping, MedPAO-VL offers a transparent and clinically viable alternative for automated structured radiology report generation.

title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

title: In the Guise of Correction: How Framing and Cultural Adaptation Erode LLM Safety on Real-World Criminal Cases
summary: Existing safety benchmarks rely largely on synthetic prompts with loosely grounded taxonomies and offer little focused analysis of severe crime categories. We introduce GUISE, a benchmark of criminal-assistance scenarios sourced from real-world cases and organised under a taxonomy from the UNODC International Classification of Crime for Statistical Purposes (ICCS). Each scenario is rendered under three linguistic framings and evaluated across five distinct cultures. Using our proposed two-tier evaluation framework, which judges both harmfulness and operational uplift, we find that: (i) framing alone drives unsafe compliance, with the mean unsafe compliance rate rising from 28.9% under direct requests to 66.4% under correction seeking (peaking at 97.3%; p < 0.05), as models correcting deliberately distorted details supply executable criminal steps; (ii) culturally adapted prompts elicit significantly more unsafe compliance than literal translations of the same requests in all four non-English languages (+7 to +18 points), a risk that translation-based benchmarks miss; and (iii) unsafe responses from the least-safe models carry strong Anglocentric registers, and the extent of this leakage increases monotonically with response harmfulness ($ρ$ = 0.46 to 0.63 across languages, all p < 0.001). GUISE offers a grounded resource and fine-grained diagnostics for strengthening refusal alignment across languages and cultures. We publish our code and data to facilitate future research.

title: Synthetic populations for epidemic, demographic and mobility modeling
summary:
Synthetic populations are essential for individual-based simulations, such as agent-based models, enabling the evaluation of policy interventions for epidemic control, demographic studies and mobility management, to mention a few. Existing synthetic populations are often designed for specific settings and rarely combine nationwide coverage with realistic and explicit spatial detail. This limits their ability to represent realistic spatial relationships and interplay between households, workplaces, leisure activities, and mobility patterns, reducing models utility for targeted decision-making.
  Here, we present a harmonized dataset of synthetic populations taking as case studies Spain, France, and Italy. Despite heterogeneous census data sources and formats, we release a unified data structure ensuring consistency and interoperability. The synthetic population generation pipeline reproduces household composition, population density, age-sex structure, and occupation distribution at census-tract level, enriched with municipality-level commuting flows and economic activity patterns. Country-specific pre-processing, statistical calibration, and data integration produce coherent demographic and spatial characteristics suitable for large-scale, country-agnostic simulations.
  As the pipeline relies on publicly available census data, it is readily extensible to other countries, supporting high-resolution modeling of infectious diseases, hazard exposure, demographic analysis, and urban mobility.

title: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World
summary: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.

title: DINO-FIL: Multi-Layer Transformer Fusion for Generative Inpainting Forgery Localization
summary: We propose DINO-FIL, a transformer-based framework for pixel-level localization of generative image forgeries. The method leverages multi-layer representations from a pretrained DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 encoder combined with a lightweight fusion decoder to capture both semantic structure and fine-grained texture inconsistencies introduced by image editing. By aggregating intermediate transformer features across depths, the model improves sensitivity to subtle, spatially localized artifacts that are often missed by standard single-layer approaches. We evaluate DINO-FIL in a cross-dataset setting, training on B-Free and testing on Beyond the Brush, CocoGlide, TGIF, and SAGI-D. The model achieves strong generalization, outperforming existing baselines on average and on four of five evaluated datasets, while maintaining a high true negative rate on pristine images.

title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
summary: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.

title: Localization induced by Sinai disorder in mass-exchange models
summary: We introduce a conservative continuous-mass-exchange model with quenched disorder in the splitting laws on the bonds of a finite segment. Although the dynamics is generically irreversible, its stationary mean mass profile remarkably turns out to be exactly solvable through an associated birth-and-death chain and has a Gibbs representation in terms of a simple random-walk potential. If $N$ is the number of bonds and $β$ measures the strength of disorder, the parameter $β\sqrt N$ separates an asymptotically flat profile, a Brownian crossover, and a profile localized near the global minimum. We characterize the fluctuations of macroscopic masses and identify arcsine laws for the localization centre, the competition between left and right valleys, and the disorder-averaged mass measure. Furthermore, for the extremal masses, we discuss the emergent limiting random variable in terms of the literature linking finite RW paths seen from its minimum to infinite-horizon walks conditioned to stay positive. Finally, in proximity of the localization transition point $β=0$, we show that the inverse participation ratio for the extremal masses give rises to a scaling with decay of order $k^{-3/2}$ consistent with the scaling limit of the latter conditioned walk. In the same limit, the inverse participation ratio shows a scaling form.

title: ALMA2040: The High-Redshift Circumgalactic Medium. Imaging the fueling and feedback of galaxies in the early universe
summary: Galaxies do not form in isolation, but rather as part of a wider interconnected web mediated at their interface by an extended gaseous atmosphere - the Circum-Galactic Medium (CGM). This dynamic and multiphase region is fed and shaped by gas inflows and mergers from the intergalactic medium and by feedback-driven outflows and radiation from the central galaxy. The CGM is imprinted by the past, present and future evolution of its central galaxy and environment. The cool atomic and molecular phases are of particular interest as they dominate the mass budget of outflows and provide a reservoir of direct star forming fuel for the galaxy to accrete. In the early universe where accretion rates, mergers, and feedback processes peak, the cycle of gas through the CGM is most vigorous. Sub-mm observations have detected cold gas in extended halos and gas flows around high redshift galaxies but are thus far limited to the most massive, extreme or gravitationally lensed sources, using just a handful of the strongest emission and absorption lines. A significant increase ($5-10\times$) in spectral line sensitivity compared with the current ALMA is needed to push physical scales, densities and properties to a new regime. We present three key scientific cases for an ALMA2040 telescope: (i) direct imaging of extended [CII]-traced CGM halos around Milky-Way-progenitor galaxies at $z=4$-8; (ii) resolved detection of cold, clumpy outflows on $\sim$100 pc scales tied to individual star-forming clumps; and (iii) multi-species/-transition emission and absorption diagnostics that jointly constrain the density, chemistry, and radiation fields permeating the cool CGM and its multiphase gas flows.

title: From local chemistry to galactic evolution: unlocking the power of interstellar isotopes with ALMA2040
summary: Molecular isotopic ratios provide a unique window into the chemical evolution of the interstellar medium, linking stellar nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution to the physical and chemical processes shaping molecular clouds, star-forming regions, and planetary systems. However, molecular isotopic ratios do not necessarily trace the underlying elemental composition, as chemical isotopic fractionation, isotope-selective photodissociation, grain chemistry, and radiative-transfer effects can significantly alter the observed values. Disentangling these effects requires simultaneous observations of multiple transitions, isotope systems and molecular families, including rare, doubly, and multiply substituted isotopologues involving D, $^{13}$C, $^{15}$N, $^{17,18}$O, $^{29,30}$Si, and $^{33,34,36}$S (e.g., $^{13}$C$^{15}$N, $^{13}$C$^{34}$S, and $^{13}$C$^{18}$O). ALMA2040, with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sensitivity and at least 512 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth, will make these species accessible across statistically significant samples of Galactic and nearby extragalactic sources. By enabling systematic isotopic inventories from molecular clouds and prestellar cores to protoplanetary systems, across the Milky Way and in external galaxies, ALMA2040 will establish molecular isotopes as quantitative probes of chemical inheritance, stellar nucleosynthesis, and galaxy evolution, disentangling local chemical processing from the large-scale evolution of matter from stars to new planetary systems.

title: Scaling up statistical model checking of cyber-physical systems via algorithm ensemble and parallel simulations over HPC infrastructures
summary: Model-based formal verification of industry-relevant Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) is often a computationally prohibitive task. In most cases, the complexity of the models precludes any prospect of symbolic analysis, leaving numerical simulation as the only viable option. Unfortunately, exhaustive simulation of a CPS model over the entire set of plausible operational scenarios is rarely possible in practice, and alternative strategies such as Statistical Model Checking (SMC) must be used instead. In this article, we show that the number of model simulations (samples) required by SMC techniques to converge can be significantly reduced by considering multiple (an ensemble of) Adaptive Stopping Algorithms (SAs) at once, and that the simulations themselves (by far the most expensive step of the entire workload) can be efficiently sped up by exploiting massively parallel platforms. With three industry-scale CPS models, we experimentally show that the use of an ensemble of two state-of-the-art SAs (AA and EBGStop) may require dozens of millions fewer samples when compared to running a single algorithm, with reductions in sample size of up to 78%. Furthermore, we show that our implementation, by massively parallelizing system model simulations on a HPC infrastructure, yields speed-ups for the completion time of the verification tasks which are practically linear with respect to the number of computational nodes, thus achieving an efficiency of virtually 100%, even on very large platforms. This makes it possible to complete tasks of model-based SMC verification for complex CPSs in a matter of hours or days, whereas a naïve sequential execution would require from months to many years.

title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
summary: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research
summary: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question. A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs, where Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reaches RC4 in only 32.7% of attempts. Across the benchmark, 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fall short of RC4, while all seven models reach RC4 on substantially fewer tasks in all three runs than in at least one. Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure. Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.

title: Q($γ_H$): Entropy-Guided Horizon Mixing in Multi-Discount Q-Learning
summary: A fixed discount factor in Q-learning imposes a single planning horizon throughout training, despite the differing demands of early exploration and long-term credit assignment. We propose Q($γ_H$), a multi-horizon Q-learning framework that maintains multiple discount-specific heads and adaptively combines them at control time using an entropy-derived confidence signal. The resulting state-dependent mixing weights shift control from shorter- to longer-horizon heads as policy confidence increases, enabling adaptive horizon mixing without modifying individual Bellman updates. Across classical control and deep reinforcement-learning benchmarks, Q($γ_H$) shows its strongest improvements on delayed-credit tasks relative to strong fixed-discount baselines. By decoupling horizon adaptation from the underlying learning updates, Q($γ_H$) provides a lightweight framework for adaptive planning-horizon control in reinforcement learning, avoiding the need for manual discount-factor selection while remaining compatible with standard value-learning methods.

title: Bias Mitigation in Audio-Enabled LLMs through Adversarial Training and Distillation Methods
summary: Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the model's accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues may lead to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models' perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted. However, in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.

title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
summary: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.

title: Beyond Generation: Using Multimodal LLMs as Detectors of LLM-Generated Deepfake Facial Images
summary: As image generation models become increasingly capable of producing highly realistic content, traditional forensic techniques are struggling to keep up. This paper investigates whether MLLMs can instead be used as a form of forensic analysis by identifying synthetic media. Specifically, the study aims to determine whether these models detect fake images by recognising physical inconsistencies, or whether they rely on digital artefacts such as embedded watermarks.Six MLLMs: GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5, Gemini 3, and Seed 1.6, are benchmarked using a dataset of 400 images. Fifty images are authentic photographs, while the remaining 350 are generated using seven leading image models: Gemini 3, Gemini 2.5, Flux.2 Pro, GPT-Image-1, GPT-Image-1.5, Seedream 4.0, and Seedream 4.5. The evaluation is structured in three stages: single-image classification, pairwise comparison, and a focused "self-detection" experiment on Gemini. Several MLLMs achieved a high detection accuracy, with GPT-5.2 reaching a peak of 97.9% in the pairwise experiment, against specific generators and an overall mean pairwise accuracy of 82.5% by identifying structural or physical inconsistencies within images. However, results from the self-detection experiment indicate that the presence of invisible SynthID watermarks leads to a 10% reduction in Gemini's detection accuracy compared to the clean control group. One possible explanation is that SynthID embedding reduces some of the visible artefacts the models rely on for detection.These results imply that MLLMs can detect structural artefacts without relying on watermarks, but performance varies substantially across model generations. The findings from comparison C5 also suggest that SynthID embedding may suppress some of the structural artefacts used during detection.

title: Model-Driven Deep Learning for Distributed Detection with Low-Bit Quantization
summary: Distributed detection plays a fundamental role in communication-efficient collaborative inference over large-scale networks, where spatially distributed nodes must cooperate using severely quantized messages due to bandwidth constraints. While low-bit quantization is essential for reducing communication overhead, it can significantly degrade detection performance, particularly when prior knowledge of observation noise is unavailable. To address this challenge, we propose a model-driven deep learning framework for distributed detection with low-bit quantization. For fixed local quantizers, we first derive the exact finite-sensor maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection error and prove that, under conditionally independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, independent local randomizations, and a common quantization-level constraint, identical quantizers preserve the supremum of the average network Chernoff information. Guided by these results, we develop a binary probabilistic quantizer with a trainable neural probability controller and design a tree-structured probabilistic quantizer for scalable multi-bit quantization. The exact finite-sensor MAP error provides the training objective for the binary quantizer, while we derive a computationally tractable Bhattacharyya surrogate objective for training the multi-bit quantizer. For both cases, we derive analytical MAP fusion rules based on the class-conditional probability mass functions (PMFs) of the quantized messages. When the observation statistics are unknown, these PMFs are estimated from held-out labeled data, yielding plug-in MAP detectors. Simulation results show that the proposed method approaches centralized-oracle performance at higher quantization resolutions and remains effective under changes in network size and test-time signal amplitude.

title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
summary: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.

title: Multi-Higgs production from a theory of varying Higgs quartic and top Yukawa couplings
summary: We study the collider phenomenology of a theory in which the Higgs quartic self-coupling and the top Yukawa coupling are \textit{varying couplings}, which arise dynamically from two scalar fields, $φ_1$ and $φ_2$. Depending on the scalar masses relative to twice the top-quark mass, the heavy scalars decay mainly to Higgs boson pairs ($hh$) or to top-quark pairs ($t\bar t$), giving two distinct signatures. We find sizeable cross sections for resonant $hh$ production, and also for the background-suppressed process with three Higgs bosons ($hhh$) from associated production, $pp \to hφ_i \to hhh$. By recasting ATLAS resonance searches, we set bounds on the effective new-physics scales $Λ_1$ and $Λ_2$ at the TeV scale. We also show that the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) will probe this parameter space further, through combined measurements of the $hh$, $t\bar t$ and multi-Higgs channels. This gives a strong, multi-channel test of whether the electroweak sector has a dynamical origin.

title: The Dormant Spiking Neuron: A State-Driven Mechanism for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.

title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
summary: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale--accountability tradeoff: larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric.
